description: Six AI engineering students from Buenos Aires. Our name is a reminder: good tools make people wiser, they don't replace them. For Field Shift we asked an agronomist about a record El Niño year: "We all know the forecast already." So we built Cropilot, which uses NASA data to find the past seasons that started like this one. On the way: computer vision (U-Net) on NASA HLS imagery to map crops, a reinforcement-learning planner checked against an exact solver and a source-citing LLM assistant.
summary: Cropilot helps agronomists explore crop rotations using NASA weather and satellite data, Argentine agricultural records and transparent historical scenarios. Instead of presenting one forecast, it finds past campaigns that started under similar El Nino and regional soil-moisture conditions, then shows how alternative rotations performed. Public cases connect climate context, crop history, water simulations and economic trade-offs with their sources and limitations. An interactive planner compares fixed rotations, exact dynamic programming and Q-learning on held-out campaigns, while an evidence-linked assistant explains results by text or AI-generated voice. Cropilot supports professional judgment: regional estimates are not field measurements, scenarios are not agronomic recommendations, and unproven benefits remain explicit.
details:
Cropilot connects historical evidence to the questions agronomists face when planning a rotation: which previous campaigns resemble the current conditions, what happened to different crops, and what changes when priorities shift toward water or soil cover?

The public website provides regional cases with a national context map, historical campaign comparisons, rotation strategies, field crop maps where available, and expandable source references. NASA POWER supplies regional daily meteorology and root-zone soil-wetness context. NASA HLS L30/S30 imagery supports crop mapping in Pergamino and Parana, using INTA crop maps as reference labels and Fields of The World field outlines. NOAA ONI, MAGyP agricultural estimates and cost reports, SoilGrids, FAO methods and cited agronomic literature provide complementary evidence.

The water comparisons replay historical weather through a physical model under explicit soil-depth, initial-water and sowing-date scenarios. The live planner lets signed-in users set priorities for gross margin, crop water deficit, bare-soil days, rain on bare soil and drainage over one to five campaigns. It builds a decision process from historical training campaigns, solves it with dynamic programming, trains Q-learning agents and compares policies with fixed rotations on held-out campaigns. We report negative and inconclusive results as well as positive ones; we do not claim a demonstrated resilience advantage of RL over simple policies.

An assistant answers questions using the published evidence and preserves the distinction between original data, modeled outputs, scenario assumptions and missing information. It is available through text and labeled AI-generated speech. Public MCP tools expose the same evidence to compatible assistants, and a mobile companion reuses the shared services.

The implementation uses Python, FastAPI, NumPy and scientific ML libraries, React/TypeScript, MapLibre, PostgreSQL and containerized deployment. Crop-mapping and research models use LightGBM and PyTorch; selected research workloads ran on an RTX 3090. OpenAI and Anthropic tools assisted development and research and are credited in the public attribution register.

The intended benefit is a more transparent conversation between agronomist and producer about historical risks and trade-offs. Regional climate cells are not field sensors; crop classification agreement is not field validation; water drainage is not a validated flood-loss estimate. Missing observations, limited geographic modules and model uncertainty are visible. Every output is a scenario for professional review, not an operational agronomic recommendation.

OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude/Claude Code assisted research, implementation, analysis, documentation and testing at the direction of the team. OpenAI models generate the evidence-linked assistant responses and its labeled synthetic speech. Original NASA and third-party datasets retain their provider attribution. AI-assisted code and team-derived simulations and classifications are identified separately from observations. Product screen recordings are captures of the running application.

NASA JPL: Some Algorithms for Polygons on a Sphere - field-map area calculation reference
